## Abstract

Molecular aberrations have been incorporated into tumor classification guidelines of meningioma. TERT-promoter (TERTp) mutation is considered to associate with worse prognosis and designated a World Health Organization (WHO) grade 3 biomarker. However, it remains unclear whether TERTp mutation is context-dependent, with other co-occurring alterations potentially driving its association with prognosis. We sought to characterize the role of TERTp mutation in meningioma and guide TERTp sequencing.

We identified 1492 patients of all ages who received surgery for meningioma across 14 medical centers in the United States, Canada, and Germany. Patients were eligible if they had post-surgical clinical and/or radiographic assessment of the resection site and TERTp status evaluated by November 1, 2024. Multi-modal profiling was used to assess TERTp mutation, focal gene alterations, including CDKN2A/B loss, and copy number alterations. An adjusted WHO grade was calculated for TERTp-mutant meningiomas, incorporating all WHO criteria except TERTp status. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox proportional hazard models were used to quantify the impact of TERTp mutation on the endpoints of overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) across adjusted WHO grade and co-occurring molecular alterations.

We identified 64 TERTp-mutant meningioma patients (51·6% female, median age 67 years, IQR 60–75 years) and 1428 TERTp-wildtype patients (67·6% female, median age 59, IQR 48–70). The TERTp-mutant patients had a 5-year OS (49·4%, 95% CI: 33·7%-72·4%) and 5-year RFS (27·6%, 95%CI: 16.8%-45.5%) resembling that of WHO grade 3 TERTp-wildtype patients. However, the TERTp-mutant group had heterogenous histological grading and was enriched for aggressive molecular features, with 1p loss present in 77·2% (44/57) and CDKN2A/B loss in 41·4% (24/58) of profiled tumors. Adjusting tumor grade revealed a subset of TERTp-mutant meningiomas that were more molecularly and clinically benign. Among TERTp-mutant tumors, CDKN2A/B loss played a defining role in stratifying tumor behavior. Multivariable analysis confirmed this, with CDKN2A/B loss being significantly associated with shorter survival (HR: 3·04, 95%CI: 1·67–5·52, p<0·001) and faster time to recurrence (HR: 5·22, 95%CI: 3·10–8·79, p<0·001), while TERTp-mutation did not independently affect OS (HR: 1·00, 95%CI: 0·53–1·87, p=0·99) or RFS (HR: 1·17, 95%CI: 0·75–1·83, p=0·49). Sequencing for TERTp-mutation demonstrated clinical impact only among histologically WHO grade 2 meningiomas.

The indolent behavior of certain TERTp-mutant meningiomas suggests that TERTp mutation is not sufficient to assign the most aggressive meningioma grade. Instead, TERT sequencing may offer prognostic utility identifying high-risk cases amongst WHO grade 2 meningiomas.

## Introduction

Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumors in adults, with clinical management largely guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) grading scheme.1 Surgery is typically first-line treatment, with adjuvant radiation and salvage treatment decisions influenced by WHO grade, particularly in higher-grade tumors or when gross total resection (GTR) is not achieved.2,3 Accurate grading is therefore critical to determine recurrence risk and appropriate management.

Routine molecular profiling has transformed WHO tumor classifications, which rely on histopathology and are prone to interobserver variability and sampling bias.4,5 Large-scale efforts have identified prognostic markers including copy number alterations, CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion, and telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter (TERTp) mutation, that correlate with outcomes.4,6–10 Recent studies also link hemizygous CDKN2A/B loss with poor prognosis in meningioma.9,11,12 Accordingly, the 2021 WHO Classification designates TERTp mutation or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion as sufficient for grade 3 meningioma.2

TERTp mutations maintain telomere length and enable indefinite proliferation.13 While TERTp mutation is a key driver in systemic cancers, its impact on prognosis varies across central nervous system (CNS) cancers.14–18 In meningioma, TERTp mutations are rare and associate with poor prognosis.7,19–22 Most studies, however, are single-institutional, with limited sample size and lack external validation. Some report TERTp mutation to be a marker of disease progression7,19,22, while others suggest its impact is limited to anaplastic meningiomas.2020 In most studies, TERTp mutations were present at initial diagnosis20,23, while others suggest they are acquired as part of malignant progression, highlighting the lack of consensus regarding the role of TERTp mutation in meningioma.24

Despite these uncertainties, TERTp mutation remains sufficient for WHO grade 3 designation, potentially influencing subsequent treatment. We hypothesize that upgrading meningiomas based solely on TERTp mutation may lead to unnecessary aggressive treatments and associated morbidity. Here, we assemble an international, multi-institutional cohort of 1492 meningiomas to (1) determine the prognostic impact of TERTp mutations, (2) investigate the clinical and molecular landscape of TERTp-mutant meningiomas, and (3) propose guidelines regarding for incorporating TERTp sequencing into clinical management.

## Methods

### Study design and participants

In this retrospective, multicenter analysis, we collected data from fourteen institutions (Baylor College of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Massachusetts General Hospital, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Mount Sinai, Northwestern University, New York University, UCSF, University Hospital Heidelberg, University Medical Center Hamburg, University of Pennsylvania, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Yale) (Figure 1, appendix p 1). Patients of all ages were included if they had surgical resection performed for meningioma, post-surgical clinical and/or radiographic assessment of the resection site, and TERTp status evaluated by November 1, 2024. Our final study cohort included 1492 meningioma samples from unique patients, after excluding 54 samples representing subsequent recurrences or multi-focal samples from the same patient. Available demographic, clinical, and molecular data were compiled for each case. This study was approved by the Brigham and Women’s Hospital and NYU Langone Institutional Review Boards and conducted according to their guidelines, with waivers issued for written informed consent given the retrospective nature of this analysis. No patient representatives were formally involved in shaping this analysis.

### Procedures

Histopathologic review was performed by board-certified neuropathologists at each institution, following the WHO tumor classification for meningioma. Mitotic count (number of mitoses per 10 high-powered fields) and Ki-67 index (immunohistochemistry staining for Ki-67 protein) were extracted from pathology records, with the midpoint of reported ranges used for analysis. Unclear Ki-67 metrics were excluded. For TERTp-wildtype meningiomas, WHO grade was assigned according to the WHO Classification (2007, 2016, or 2021) at the time of diagnosis with formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples (FFPE). In select cases where data was acquired for research, grade was re-assigned according to the 2021 WHO Classification. To assess TERTp mutation impact, all TERTp-mutant meningiomas were classified by two schemes: 1) the 2021 WHO tumor classification, which assigns all TERTp tumors to grade 3, and 2) an ‘adjusted WHO grade’ that excludes TERTp upgrading.

Frozen or FFPE meningioma samples underwent TERTp sequencing via institutionally validated targeted Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), whole exome sequencing (WES), or droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) platforms (appendix p1). No clinical outcome endpoints were present at the time of molecular assessment. Chromosome copy number (CN) profiles were generated from genome-wide microarray or DNA methylation using the conumee R package. A molecularly Integrated Grade (IG) described for meningioma classification was calculated in a subset of cases (n=611) based on mitotic count, loss of CDKN2A/B, and chromosomal arm losses (1p, 3p, 4p/q, 6p/q, 10p/q, 14q, 18p/q, 19p/q).9 Tumors missing any Integrated Grade component were excluded from IG analysis unless the criteria for Integrated Grade 3 were already met. The full cohort mutational and copy number landscape is provided in appendix p3.

### Outcomes

Clinical history, demographics, tumor location, extent of resection, radiographic recurrence, and overall survival were collected from clinical charts. Patient sex, race, and/or ethnicity (where applicable) was defined by self-report. Extent of surgical resection was defined as gross total resection (GTR, complete macroscopic tumor removal) or subtotal resection (STR) based on neurosurgeon judgment and post-operative MRI. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS), defined as time from surgery to radiographic recurrence (or progression for STR cases). This was determined by a multidisciplinary team at each institution. The secondary endpoint was overall survival (OS), defined as time from surgery to death.

### Statistical Analysis

Sample size was not selected a priori and was maximized to detect TERTp mutant meningiomas. Summary measures were calculated for demographic and clinical variables. OS and RFS distributions were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves and compared by log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. This included sub-stratification by TERTp status, histological grading, extent of resection, and additional molecular alterations like CDKN2A/B loss. Patients were censored at last follow-up, presence of meningioma recurrence (RFS) or death (OS). No informative censoring was performed. Prognostic significance was assessed using univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models for RFS and OS. The proportional hazard assumption was met, confirmed through visual inspection, Univariable analyses included: age (continuous), sex (male vs. female), adjusted WHO grade (high (2/3) vs. low (1)), extent of resection (GTR vs. STR), location (skull base vs. non-skull base), treatment with adjuvant radiation, primary (vs. recurrent) status, chromosome 1p loss, chromosome 22q loss, homozygous CDKN2A/B loss, and TERTp status. Adjusted WHO grade was used to avoid collinearity with TERTp status. Multivariable Cox models included all parameters significant in univariable analysis after Bonferroni correction (p<0.05).

Propensity score matching (PSM) was conducted for OS and RFS to address confounders. Propensity scores were calculated by logistic regression without replacement, using covariates: age, sex, adjusted WHO grade (1, 2, or 3), extent of resection, location, adjuvant radiation, and primary (vs. recurrent) status. A 10:1 nearest neighbor matching algorithm was used to pair each TERTp-mutant meningioma with 10 TERTp-wildtype meningiomas. Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test as well as cox proportional hazards models compared RFS and OS between groups. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.05. All statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.3.2).

### Role of the funding source

Study funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.

## Results

Amongst 1492 meningiomas collected up to November 1, 2024, 64 (4·3%) were TERTp-mutant (33 (51·6%) of 64 female, median age 67 years, IQR 60–75 years) and 1428 (95·7%) were TERTp-wildtype (965 (67·6%) of 1428 female, median age 59, IQR 48–70). Data on race was inconsistently reported and thus excluded. Of the 1428 TERTp-wildtype cases, 911 (63·8%) meningiomas were WHO grade 1, 476 (33·3%) grade 2, and 41 (2·9%) grade 3 (Table 1). All TERTp mutant meningiomas were WHO grade 3 by definition. When grading was adjusted to exclude TERTp status, of the 64 TERTp mutant meningiomas, 12 TERTp-mutant meningiomas (18·8%) were adjusted grade 1, 17 (26·6%) adjusted to grade 2, and 35 (54·7%) remained as grade 3.

TERTp-mutant meningiomas were enriched for aggressive histological features compared to the TERTp-wildtype cases, with a median mitoses per high powered field (HPF) of 8·0 (IQR 4·3–20·0) and a median Ki-67 index of 15·0% (IQR 7·3–20·0) (Table 1, Figure 2A). TERTp-mutant meningiomas more often localized to the lateral convexity (44·0% (22/50)) or falcine/parasagittal region (32·0% (16/50)) than to the skull base (14·0% (7/50): lateral skull base 10·0% (5/50), midline skull base 4·0% (2/50)) (Table 1). Median follow-up was 2·3 years (IQR 1·0–5·0 years); 2·0 years (IQR 0·7–3·2) for TERTp-mutant and 2·4 years (IQR 1·0–5·0) for TERTp-wildtype tumors.

On aggregate comparison, OS and RFS for TERTp-mutant meningioma were significantly worse compared to low and intermediate grade TERTp-wildtype cases (Figure 2B–C). OS was assessed in 57 TERTp-mutant (18 deaths) and 1426 TERTp-wildtype (130 deaths) cases while RFS was assessed in 63 TERTp-mutant (41 recurred) and 1422 TERTp-wildtype (257 recurred) cases (Figure 1). TERTp-mutant 5-year OS was 49·4% (95% Confidence Interval (CI): 33·7%-72·4%), significantly less than TERTp-wildtype grade 1 (92·5%, 95%CI: 90·0%-95·0%, p<0·001) and grade 2 (81·4%, 95%CI: 76·5%-86·6%, p<0·0001) cases. TERTp-mutant tumors also showed a lower 5-year RFS rate (27·6%, 95%CI: 16.8%-45.5%) compared to TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 1 (80·3%, 95%CI: 76·6%-84·0%, p<0·0001) and WHO grade 2 (57·5%, 95%CI: 50·4%-65·6%, p<0·0001) cases. The TERTp-mutant cohort shared a similar OS and RFS to TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 3 meningiomas (5-year OS 32·3%, 95%CI: 17·2%-60·5%, p=0·28, 5-year RFS 14·3%, 95%CI: 5·8%-35·2%, p=0·28, Figure 2B–C).

Among cases that received GTR, TERTp-mutant meningiomas had an intermediate clinical phenotype. OS was assessed in 29 GTR TERTp-mutant and 965 GTR TERTp-wildtype cases while RFS was assessed in 32 TERTp-mutant and 963 TERTp-wildtype cases The 5-year OS of GTR TERTp-mutant cases was 68·5% (95%CI: 47·3%-99·2%), which did not significantly differ from TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 2 cases (p=0.27, appendix p 4). Notably, this was higher than 5-year survival of all TERTp-mutant cases (49·3%, 95%CI: 33·7%-72·4%, Figure 2B), suggesting heterogeneous intersecting effects with TERTp-mutation. Further, TERTp-mutant cases with GTR (5-year RFS 36·6%, 95%CI: 20·7%-64·8%) showed RFS that was worse than WHO grade 2 TERTp-wildtype cases with GTR (5-year RFS 64·4%, 95%CI: 55·7%-74·5%) and appeared better than WHO grade 3 TERTp-wildtype cases with GTR (5-year RFS 16·8%, 95%CI: 6·0%-46·9%, p=0·063, appendix p 4), but was not statistically significant. Similar to OS, TERTp-mutant cases with GTR had differing 5-year RFS compared to all TERTp-mutant cases. This intermediate effect observed among GTR TERTp-mutant cases may suggest that the prognostic effect of TERTp mutation is dependent on additional clinical variables as opposed to an absolute marker of aggressiveness.

Given the differential TERTp-mutant outcomes across extent of resection, we evaluated the histological variability within TERTp-mutant cases. Stratifying the TERTp-mutant cohort using the ‘adjusted WHO grade,’ defined as 2021 WHO grade without upgrading cases based on TERTp status, revealed differential clinical outcomes (57 assessed for OS, 63 for RFS). While adjusted WHO grade 3 TERTp-mutant meningiomas did not show a statistically significant difference (p=0·093, Figure 3A) towards worse OS (5-year survival 33·1%, 95%CI: 15·7%-70·1%) compared with adjusted WHO grade 1 TERTp-mutant meningiomas (5-year survival 77·8%, 95%CI: 54·9%-100%), recurrence differed significantly between these groups. Adjusted WHO grade 3 TERTp-mutant meningiomas having a 5-year RFS of 10·2% (95%CI: 3·1%-33·7%), compared to 72·7% (95%CI: 50·6%-100%) for adjusted WHO grade 1 TERTp-mutant meningiomas (p=0·0041, Figure 3C). When adjusted TERTp-mutant cases were compared to TERTp-wildtype cases, there was no significant difference in OS across each grade comparison (Figure 3B). However, for recurrence, a significant difference emerged between adjusted WHO grade 2 TERTp-mutant meningiomas (5-year RFS 29·6%, 95%CI: 10·3%-85·6%) and WHO grade 2 TERTp-wildtype meningiomas (5-year RFS 57·5%, 95%CI: 50·4%-65·6%, p=0·028, Figure 3D). These findings remained consistent when examining cases that only received GTR (appendix p 4). The distinct outcomes across TERTp-mutant tumors stratified by their original histological grade further indicate that TERTp mutation may not uniformly confer a poor prognosis.

We next examined the molecular background of TERTp-mutant meningiomas, revealing the complexity of co-occurring mutations and copy number alterations. The majority of TERTp-mutant meningiomas (53 of 59 meningiomas, 89·8%), had >1 copy number alteration, many of which are associated with a high risk of recurrence (Figure 2A).9,25 Loss of chromosome 1p, a feature associated with meningioma aggressiveness, was observed in 77·2% (44 of 57) of TERTp-mutant meningiomas. Additional frequent copy number losses were seen on chromosomes 3p (14·5%, 8 of 55), 4p (27·3%, 15 of 55), 4q (16·4%, 9 of 55), 6p (14·3%, 8 of 56), 6q (30·4%, 17 of 56), 10q (29·1%, 16 of 55), 14q (38·6%, 22 of 57), 18q (35·7%, 20 of 56), 19p (7·3%, 4 of 55), and 22q (84·5%, 49 of 58) (Figure 2A). Concurrent loss of chromosomes 1p and 22q has also been proposed as a molecular criterion of higher risk meningioma.26 27 Within our TERTp-mutant meningiomas, we observed minimal divergence between 1p and 22q loss. Only 6·8% (3 of 44) of TERTp-mutant meningiomas with chromosome 1p loss did not have concurrent chromosome 22q loss. CDKN2A/B homozygous loss, another alteration linked with tumor recurrence, was present in 31·7% (20 of 63) of TERTp-mutant meningiomas, compared to 1·7% (22 of 1323) of TERTp-wildtype meningiomas (appendix p 3, Table 1). An additional 7·0% (4 of 57) of TERTp-mutant meningiomas had a hemizygous loss of CDKN2A/B. 62·5% (35 of 56) of TERTp-mutant meningiomas showed concurrent NF2 loss. Additional concurrent mutations were also seen in AKT1 (7·5%, 4 of 53), SMO (7·5%, 4 of 53), TRAF7 (2·1%, 1 of 47), and PIK3CA (1·9%, 1 of 53).

TERTp-mutant meningiomas diverged in OS and RFS when considering molecular features such as CDKN2A/B homozygous/hemizygous loss (Figure 4A–B). TERTp-mutant meningiomas with intact CDKN2A/B had significantly longer survival (5-year survival 71·3%, 95%CI: 52·2%-97·2%) compared to those with any CDKN2A/B loss (5-year survival 16·4%, 95%CI: 3·4%-79·3%), p=0·0023, Figure 4A). This was also seen with recurrence, with TERTp-mutant CDKN2A/B intact meningiomas having a 5-year RFS rate of 52·1% (95%CI: 34·1%-79·6%) compared to 5·4% (95%CI: 0·8%-35·9%) for TERTp-mutant CDKN2A/B loss meningiomas (p<0·0001, Figure 4B). OS and RFS of TERTp-mutant CDKN2A/B loss meningiomas instead mirrored that of TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 3 tumors (5-year survival 33·3%, 95%CI: 17·2%-60·5%; 5-year RFS 14·7%, 95%CI: 6·0%-36·1%).

These differential effects across TERTp-mutant meningiomas were also seen when copy number alterations were considered through the Integrated Grade scheme, which incorporates histologic and molecular features (appendix p 5). In the TERTp-mutant cohort, 9·8% (5 of 51) were Integrated Grade 1, 25·5% (13 of 51) Integrated Grade 2, and 64·7% (33 of 51) Integrated Grade 3. Despite having a TERTp mutation, none of the Integrated Grade 1 patients passed away or experienced a recurrence during 4·8 years of median follow-up (IQR 3·1–9·3) (appendix p 5). Expectedly, these tumors were histologically benign, with all samples having <4 mitoses/10 HPF and a median Ki-67 of 3·5 (IQR 3.1–4·0). Most were adjusted WHO grade 1 (4 of 5), while one (of 5) was adjusted WHO grade 2. None of these meningiomas had concurrent CDKN2A/B or 1p loss. Three tumors in this cohort had no copy number alterations, one had isolated 22q loss, and one demonstrated loss of 22q and gain of 3p/q, 5p/q, 12p/q, and 20p/q. The location of Integrated Grade 1 TERTp-mutant meningiomas varied: 40% (2 of 5) lateral convexity, 40% (2 of 5) midline skull base, and 20% (1 of 5) falcine/parasagittal. Interestingly, all of these tumors were managed similarly with GTR and without the use of adjuvant radiation.

TERTp status is often evaluated only in the setting of meningiomas exhibiting more aggressive characteristics. To better ascertain the natural history of TERTp mutation we performed a sub-analysis of outcomes from institutions that sequence all meningiomas for TERTp status, and that included all available assayed meningiomas in our research cohort (Baylor College of Medicine, NYU Langone, and Yale). Amongst the 791 meningiomas in this cohort, 1·8% (n=14) were TERTp-mutant and 98.2% (n=777) were TERTp-wildtype. Of the TERTp-mutant meningiomas, 42·9% (6 of 14) were adjusted WHO grade 1, 28·6% (4 of 14) were adjusted WHO grade 2, and 28·6% (4 of 14) remained as adjusted WHO grade 3. Interestingly, none of the 14 TERTp-mutant meningiomas within this cohort passed away, with an average follow-up time of 4·1 (range 0·2–16·0) years (appendix p 6). TERTp-mutant meningiomas appeared to recur faster (5-year RFS 59·1%, 95%CI: 36·9%-94·5%) than TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 1 (5-year RFS 80·8%, 95%CI: 75·6%-86·3%, p=0·051), but did not reach statistical significance. The TERTp-mutant cohort appeared to have an intermediate RFS profile that was similar to both TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 2 (5-year RFS 73·4%, 95%CI: 63·8%-84·5%, p=0.15) and TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 3 (5-year RFS 16·7%, 95%CI: 2·8%-99·7%, p=0·98) meningiomas (appendix p 6). When stratified by adjusted WHO grade, there were no significant differences between TERTp-mutant and TERTp-wildtype meningiomas, though this analysis was limited by low statistical power (appendix p 6).

We performed multivariable analysis on features that were shown to be significant predictors of OS or RFS on univariable analysis (appendix p 7). While TERTp mutation was predictive of worse outcomes on univariable analysis, isolating the effect of TERTp mutation in the context of molecular and clinical features through multivariable analysis demonstrated that TERTp mutation did not independently impact OS or RFS (Figure 4C–D). When examining OS, variables associated with worse prognosis included CDKN2A/B homozygous loss (HR: 3·04, 95%CI: 1·67–5·52, p=0.0026), high adjusted WHO grade (2/3) (HR: 1·67, 95%CI: 1·08–2·57, p=0.020), and increasing age per year (HR: 1·04, 95%CI: 1·02–1·05, p<0.0001). Primary (vs. recurrent) tumor status was associated with better OS prognosis (HR: 0.27, 95%CI: 0·18–1·42, p<0.0001). TERTp mutation was not independently associated with survival (HR: 1·00, 95%CI: 0·53–1·87, p=0.99). Similarly, variables associated with a shorter time to recurrence included CDKN2A/B homozygous loss (HR: 5·22, 95%CI: 3·10–8·79, p<0.0001), chromosome 1p loss (HR: 2·99, 95%CI: 2·11–4·22, p<0.0001), male sex (HR: 1·56, 95%CI: 1·18–2·07, p=0.0020), and high adjusted WHO grade (2/3) (HR: 1·47, 95%CI: 1·03–2·11, p=0.034). Factors associated with longer time to recurrence included GTR (HR: 0·53, 95%CI: 0·39–0·71, p<0.0001) and primary (vs. recurrent) tumor status (HR: 0·50, 95%CI: 0·35–0·71, p=0.0014). In the context of these salient variables, TERTp mutation did not independently associate with recurrence (HR: 1·17, 95%CI: 0·75–1·83, p=0.49).

For added rigor, we performed PSM analysis with covariates including age, sex, adjusted WHO grade, extent of resection, location, treatment with adjuvant radiation, and primary (vs. recurrent) tumor status (appendix p 8). The PSM cohort (n=226) included 30 TERTp mutant and 196 TERTp-wildtype (81 WHO grade 1, 100 WHO grade 2, 15 WHO grade 3) meningiomas. Within the PSM cohort, TERTp did not independently associate with OS (HR: 1·67, 95%CI: 0·19–1·86, p=0·37) or RFS (HR: 0·98, 95%CI: 0·54–1·92, p=0.96). While statistical power was limited in this smaller cohort, outcomes in OS and RFS closely resembled those seen in the GTR cohort, with TERTp-mutant meningiomas showing an intermediate clinical phenotype that varies based upon histologic grade (appendix p 8).

## Discussion

Accurate, evidence-based WHO grading is necessary for meningioma management. Given interobserver variability in histopathological assessment, CDKN2A/B homozygous loss and TERTp mutation were incorporated into WHO guidelines as biomarkers of grade 3 behavior. Our analysis of 1,492 meningiomas with TERTp status suggests TERTp mutation is not independently predictive of malignancy in meningioma.

The true incidence of TERTp mutation is difficult to ascertain due to selection bias. In our cohort, most institutions only evaluated a subset of histologically aggressive meningiomas for TERTp status due to cost restrictions and uncertain impact. The incidence of TERTp mutation amongst the institutions which evaluate all resected meningiomas for TERTp status was 1·8%, notably lower than the TERTp incidence across the full cohort (4·5%) and reported in the literature (4·5–7·2).7,19,21 This estimate of 1·8% likely exceeds the true incidence as these institutions are tertiary academic centers, with a referral bias in meningiomas. Thus, we are unable to make epidemiological or population-based claims related to differences in age or sex between TERTp-mutant and TERTp-wildtype meningiomas.

TERTp-mutant meningiomas are histologically and clinically heterogeneous. They showed a significant difference in survival when graded based on criteria other than TERTp status. Histologically benign adjusted WHO grade 1 TERTp-mutant meningiomas behaved similarly to TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 1 meningiomas. The outcome of TERTp-mutant meningiomas is further modified by treatment received. Those receiving gross total resection fared behaved analogous to WHO grade 2 TERTp-wildtype meningiomas in OS, significantly improved compared to tumors with subtotal resection.

TERTp mutation is rarely an isolated molecular event. Only 10·2% of TERTp-mutant meningiomas showed no copy number losses or gains, and nearly half harbor concurrent heterozygous or homozygous loss of CDKN2A/B, consistent with previous reports.2727 TERTp-mutant meningiomas lacking other biomarkers of aggressiveness show indolent behavior: five histologically and molecularly benign Integrated Grade 1 TERTp-mutant meningiomas did not experience disease recurrence after resection and without adjuvant radiation, with a median follow-up of 4·8 years. Multivariable analysis and propensity score matching analysis showed that TERTp mutation was not an independent prognostic factor of OS or RFS in meningioma. Collectively, these results suggest that negative outcomes in TERTp-mutant meningioma are frequently driven by co-occurring histologically and molecularly aggressive features more than by TERTp mutation itself.

While previous primary studies examining TERTp-mutation in meningioma were limited by small TERTp-mutant sample sizes, one meta-analysis compiling data from eight published studies reported recurrence and mortality were more likely in TERTp-mutant histologically WHO grade 1 or 2 meningiomas than in TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 3 meningiomas.28 However, this analysis did not control for extent of surgical resection, use of adjuvant radiation therapy, or the role of co-occurring molecular alterations (CDKN2A/B loss or copy number alterations). Our results suggest that CDKN2A/B status stratifies the behavior of TERTp-mutant meningiomas.

Our description of previously unrecognized indolent behavior in histologically and molecularly benign TERTp-mutant meningiomas is critical for patient management. In academic institutions sequencing all meningiomas for TERTp status, 42·9% were adjusted WHO grade 1. Per the 2021 WHO tumor classification, these tumors would be upgraded to grade 3 status, without necessarily possessing malignant behavior that warrants adjuvant radiotherapy. Our data suggests that upgrading histologically and molecularly benign TERTp-mutant meningiomas is unwarranted and risks overtreatment.

For histologically WHO grade 2 meningiomas, TERTp status offers prognostic value. While OS did not differ by TERTp status, TERTp-wildtype meningiomas showed significantly better RFS compared to mutants in both the overall cohort in the GTR cohort. The RFS of histologically WHO grade 2 TERTp-mutant meningiomas was comparable to that of TERTp-wildtype WHO grade 3 meningiomas, likely due to co-occurring molecular drivers within the TERTp-mutant tumors. Histologically grade 3 meningiomas, whether TERTp-mutant or TERTp-wildtype, are clinically aggressive and molecularly advanced, rendering TERTp status non-contributory.

Our findings inform TERTp sequencing in clinical practice, where approaches vary markedly across institutions (appendix p 1). The selectivity of the TERTp sequencing at most institutions reflects the need to balance clinically meaningful adjuncts with practical resource limitations. We outline a proposed decision-making framework for the implementation of TERTp sequencing into clinical practice (Figure 5). In the absence of therapeutics targeting TERTp, our data suggest that TERTp sequencing offers lower utility in WHO grade 1 meningiomas (histologically defined) or WHO grade 3 meningiomas (histologically or molecularly defined). Prognostic value emerges in histologically WHO grade 2 meningiomas, wherein TERTp mutation associated with worse RFS and unchanged OS. Future WHO CNS tumor classification should address these context-dependent prognostic implications.

The biological mechanism underlying the limited impact of isolated TERTp mutation in meningioma remains unclear. In many cancers, TERTp mutation mediates cell immortalization by stabilizing telomeres to prevent senescence.19,29 Its effect varies across CNS tumors. In IDH-mutant oligodendrogliomas, TERTp mutation is observed in more than 90% of tumors and associates with favorable outcomes.17,18,30 Conversely, in WHO grade 2–3 IDH-wildtype gliomas, TERTp mutation confers worse prognosis and prompts upgrade to WHO grade 4.31 In meningioma, epigenetic alterations and intratumoral heterogeneity may modulate TERT expression and detection, potentially explaining a more limited impact of TERTp mutation.19,22

Collectively, our study clarifies the role of TERTp mutation in meningioma prognostication in the context of histological grade and other biomarkers. However, there are several limitations to this analysis. Despite the large cohort, sub-analyses of TERTp-mutant tumors were limited by its low prevalence. As such, prospective external validation across additional centers sequencing for TERT is needed. Additional work is also needed to elucidate mechanisms by which TERT influences meningioma development and progression. The differential effect of TERTp mutation across histologic appearance raises questions regarding other biological mechanisms influencing tumor aggressiveness. This may include animal studies on human meningioma tissue and/or prospective tissue collection to understand molecular drivers. The number of institutions represented here may also introduce variability in meningioma sampling and reporting for clinical follow-up. We sought to reduce this effect by incorporating frequent data checks with all participating institutions to ensure accurate reporting. Nevertheless, our findings underscore the importance of context when interpreting TERTp mutations to ensure accurate risk stratification.
